Summary

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with dietary fat via chylomicrons and stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Unlike water-soluble vitamins, they accumulate in the body, making toxicity a clinical concern. Deficiency typically occurs in the setting of fat malabsorption (eg, cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, cholestasis, Crohn disease, pancreatic insufficiency).

Vitamin A

Forms & Metabolism

Sources

Plant sources: as inactive provitamin (esp. beta-carotene) in yellow and leafy vegetables (eg, spinach, kale, carrots)

Animal sources: in storage form (eg, in liver, kidney, fish, eggs, butter)

Active metabolites: retinal (vision), retinoic acid (gene transcription, differentiation), and retinol (reproductive function)

Absorbed with fat → packaged into chylomicrons → stored in hepatic stellate (Ito) cells

Retinoic acid acts as a nuclear receptor ligand → regulates gene expression (similar mechanism to steroid hormones)

Functions

Vision: retinal is a component of rhodopsin (rod photopigment) → essential for dim-light/night vision

Epithelial maintenance: promotes normal differentiation of mucus-secreting epithelial cells

Immunity: important for T-cell development and mucosal immunity

Embryogenesis: retinoic acid is critical for normal fetal development (HOX gene regulation)

Deficiency

Night blindness (nyctalopia): earliest/most classic sign; due to impaired rhodopsin regeneration

Xerophthalmia (dry eyes): can progress to corneal ulceration → blindness

Bitot spots (white foamy plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva)

Dry, scaly skin (hyperkeratosis); impaired wound healing

Increased susceptibility to infections

Toxicity

Teratogenicity: major concern; causes neural crest defects, craniofacial abnormalities

Acute toxicity: ↑ intracranial pressure (headache, papilledema), nausea, vomiting

Chronic toxicity: liver damage (hepatotoxicity), alopecia, dry skin, bone/joint pain

Isotretinoin (vitamin A derivative used for severe acne): same toxicity profile; seizures may occur in overdose; absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy

Therapeutic Uses

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (all-trans retinoic acid [ATRA])

Acne vulgaris (isotretinoin, topical retinoids)

Psoriasis (acitretin)

Vitamin D

Synthesis & Functions

Vitamin D has a complex synthesis pathway, a favorite on exams.

Vitamin D is stored primarily as 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol) in the liver and circulation, which is the major storage form and the form measured to assess vitamin D status

Active form is 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), produced in the kidney by 1α-hydroxylase and responsible for the biologic effects of vitamin D

↑ intestinal absorption of Ca²⁺ and phosphate

↑ renal reabsorption of Ca²⁺

↑ bone resorption (osteoclast activation) when calcium is low — works with PTH

Net effect: ↑ serum Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ → proper bone mineralization

Test-taking pearl: In chronic kidney disease, loss of 1α-hydroxylase activity in the kidney → ↓ calcitriol → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → renal osteodystrophy (eg, osteomalacia/osteoporosis)

Deficiency

Osteomalacia (adults): Bone pain, muscle weakness, fractures with minimal trauma (pseudo-fractures = looser zones on x-ray)

Rickets (children): Bowing of long bones (genu varum), rachitic rosary (costochondral swelling), widened wrists (metaphyseal cupping on x-ray), craniotabes, delayed fontanelle closure

Risk factor: exclusively breastfed (breast milk is low in vitamin D). Management: supplement with oral vitamin D beginning in the first months of life.

Classic Lab Pattern in Vitamin D Deficiency
LabDirectionReason
25-(OH)D₃↓Primary deficiency marker
PTH↑Secondary hyperparathyroidism compensating for low Ca²⁺
Serum Ca²⁺↓ or normalPTH partially compensates
Serum Phosphate↓PTH causes phosphaturia (phosphate wasting)
Alkaline Phosphatase↑↑ osteoblast activity from PTH stimulation

Toxicity

Caused by excessive supplementation (cannot occur from sun exposure alone)

Results in hypercalcemia: kidney stones (nephrolithiasis), constipation, confusion, nausea/vomiting, bone pain (remember the mnemonic "Stones, Bones, (abdominal) Groans, and Psychiatric Moans")

Therapeutic Uses

Rickets (children)

Osteomalacia (adults)

Osteoporosis (with calcium supplementation)

Hypocalcemia

Hypoparathyroidism

Chronic kidney disease–associated secondary hyperparathyroidism (calcitriol)

Vitamin E

Forms

α-tocopherol is the most biologically active form in humans

Functions

Primary antioxidant: α-tocopherol scavenges free radicals, protecting polyunsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes (especially RBC membranes) from oxidative damage

Works synergistically with selenium (glutathione peroxidase) to limit lipid peroxidation

Deficiency

Rare: seen in premature infants, severe fat malabsorption, abetalipoproteinemia

Hemolytic anemia (RBC membranes susceptible to oxidative damage without protective antioxidant)

Spinocerebellar ataxia (neuronal membrane damage from lipid peroxidation)

Areflexia (posterior column and peripheral nerve degeneration)

Retinopathy (in premature infants) (oxidative damage to retinal cells)

Toxicity

Relatively non-toxic even at high doses

High doses may inhibit vitamin K → impair clotting factor synthesis → ↑ bleeding risk (important drug/supplement interaction)

Therapeutic Uses

Treatment of deficiency-related hemolytic anemia

Treatment of deficiency-related neurologic dysfunction (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia)

Vitamin K

Forms & Sources

K₁ (phylloquinone): green leafy vegetables (dietary)

K₂ (menaquinone): synthesized by gut flora (GI bacteria) — clinically important because antibiotic use can deplete this source

K₃ (menadione): synthetic form; can cause hemolytic anemia in newborns — NOT used clinically

Functions

Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues on coagulation factors and anticoagulant proteins

Factors II (thrombin), VII, IX, X (pro-coagulant)

Protein C, protein S (anticoagulant; inhibit factors Va and VIIIa)

Osteocalcin (bone matrix protein; required for calcium binding in bone)

Warfarin mechanism: inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → blocks recycling of vitamin K → ↓ γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S

Deficiency

Vitamin K deficiency bleeding: neonates have low vitamin K stores (poor placental transfer) and sterile gut (no bacteria to make K₂) → prophylactic vitamin K given at birth (IM)

Prolonged PT/INR is the hallmark lab finding (extrinsic pathway factor VII has shortest half-life → most sensitive to deficiency)

Associated with antibiotic therapy (kills gut flora)

Presents as easy bruising, mucosal bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage in neonates

Toxicity

Natural K₁ and K₂ are non-toxic

Vitamin K reverses warfarin effect (used clinically for reversal)

Therapeutic Uses

Reversal of warfarin anticoagulation

Routine newborn prophylaxis to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn

Fat Malabsorption: Clinical Connections

Any condition that disrupts fat absorption will cause deficiency of all four fat-soluble vitamins (ADEK).

Fat Malabsorption Syndromes
ConditionMechanismVitamins AffectedClinical Pearl
Cystic FibrosisPancreatic exocrine insufficiency → ↓ lipase → fat malabsorptionA, D, E, KVitamin K deficiency → abnormal bleeding (↑ PT)
Celiac DiseaseVillous atrophy → ↓ absorptive surfaceA, D, E, KVitamin A deficiency → night blindness risk factor
Crohn DiseaseInflammation of terminal ileum → malabsorptionA, D, E, K + B₁₂Also causes B₁₂ deficiency (terminal ileum is site of B₁₂ absorption)
Cholestasis / Biliary Obstruction↓ bile salts → ↓ fat micelle formationA, D, E, KK deficiency → bleeding (tested with cholestyramine use)
AbetalipoproteinemiaNo chylomicrons formed → cannot absorb fat-soluble vitaminsA, D, E (most severely affected), KVitamin E deficiency → spinocerebellar ataxia, acanthocytosis
Chronic Pancreatitis↓ lipase secretionA, D, E, KVitamin A deficiency is a specific risk factor

Key Takeaways

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with fat; deficiency = think malabsorption.

Vitamin A: vision (retinal) + epithelial integrity + gene regulation (retinoic acid). Deficiency = night blindness. Toxicity = teratogen + ↑ ICP

Vitamin D: activated in liver (25-OH) then kidney (1,25-(OH)₂ = calcitriol). Deficiency = rickets/osteomalacia + secondary hyperparathyroidism. Toxicity = hypercalcemia

Vitamin E: antioxidant protecting cell membranes. Deficiency (rare) = hemolytic anemia + neurodegeneration

Vitamin K: γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X + protein C/S. Deficiency = ↑ PT/INR + bleeding. Remember: warfarin blocks K recycling

When a test question describes a patient with fat malabsorption (steatorrhea, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, Crohn disease, celiac disease, bariatric surgery), immediately consider deficiency of all four fat-soluble vitamins. The specific clinical presentation, night blindness (A), bone deformity (D), hemolytic anemia (E), or bleeding (K), will direct you to the correct vitamin. Conversely, whenever you see hypercalcemia in a patient taking supplements, always consider vitamin D toxicity

Teaching Cases

Case 1: Vitamin A Deficiency

A 40-year-old woman with celiac disease presents with worsening vision at night, especially while driving. Exam shows foamy plaques on the conjunctiva. Diagnosis: Vitamin A deficiency, refer for dietary assessment and supplementation. Key teaching: celiac disease leads to fat malabsorption, which lowers vitamin A, which impairs rhodopsin production.

Case 2: Vitamin D Deficiency / Rickets

An 18-month-old exclusively breastfed boy presents with bowed legs and swelling of the wrists. X-ray shows metaphyseal cupping. Labs: ↓ 25-(OH)D₃, ↑ PTH, ↓ phosphate, ↑ ALP. Diagnosis: Nutritional rickets. Key teaching: breast milk is low in vitamin D; supplement with oral vitamin D beginning in the first few days of life.

Case 3: Vitamin D Toxicity

A 43-year-old woman on multiple supplements presents with confusion, abdominal pain, constipation, and nephrolithiasis. Serum Ca²⁺ is elevated. Diagnosis: Vitamin D toxicity, hypercalcemia. Key teaching: treatment is to stop supplements, restrict dietary calcium, give IV fluids, ± glucocorticoids or bisphosphonates.

Case 4: Vitamin K Deficiency (Cystic Fibrosis)

A 5-month-old infant with cystic fibrosis has frequent bulky stools and is brought in for failure to thrive. The mother notes easy bruising. Labs show ↑ PT/INR. Diagnosis: vitamin K deficiency from fat malabsorption. Key teaching: fat malabsorption leads to vitamin K deficiency, which reduces γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, producing a bleeding diathesis.
